messages.subject: new functions: sort, rank, Kahan summation, ???
parts:
[re-posted on stan-dev]

sort() is definitely useful.

If we have sort(), is there a reason to also have rank()?
(That wasn't meant to be a rhetorical question.)

I'd like to see at least one realistic example where something
like Kahan summation makes a difference before including it.
Did you work on it because of an applied problem you were
having?

Does anyone else on the list have experience with this?

Did you test gradients for summation? Writing custom
gradients is critical for speed, but the gradients need to be
tested even if they're not custom. You should just be able
to use the gradient already there for sum.

Also, which signatures did you go with for sum()? It
should probably work over the same types as sort: real[],
int[], vector and row_vector.

Could you perhaps break these into two separate pull requests
(sort/rank vs. summation).

Thanks!

- Bob

> I pushed sort and rank functions to my fork now.
>
> If I have enough time, tomorrow I'll test and add them to the reference manual (as well as the float point sum precision
> functions) and then create a pull request.
>

>> But you're right --- sort() itself isn't on the list!
>>
>> Issue 1 is which types it'll work for. Probably
>> just

>> real[]
>> int[]

>> row_vector
>>
>> We would not want it to sort in place. So you'd have
>> to copy to a std::vector, apply std::sort, then return
>> (for real[] and int[]) or use to map an Eigen vector (for
>> vector and row_vector).
>>
>> The to-do list did have this:
>>
>> -- rank(v,s): number of components of v less than v[s]
>> -- ranked(v,s): s-th smallest component of v
>>
>> These are BUGS functions.
>>
>> http://www.mrc-bsu.cam.ac.uk/bugs/winbugs/manual14.pdf

>> instead of rank() and ranked()):
>>
>> http://sourceforge.net/p/mcmc-jags/discussion/610037/thread/64ce3a9c
>>
>> - Bob

> The motivation is that model I described a few weeks ago in stan-users. I'm still having a lot a trouble to deal with it.

Are you sure it's a problem with summation precision per se?

I want to understand where you need to add numbers of
vastly different scales AND the lower-order numbers
matter. That is, when do you do (1e-30 + 1e10) and
the 1e-30 term matters in the sum? We try to handle
the gradients separately, and in the usual ways to do
sums (+ and sum()), the gradients are handled independently,
so you get the right answer there even if the 1e-30 term
drops out of the sum due to underflow.

So what I'm wondering is where higher-precision summation
will make a difference.

The integrator we use to simulate the Hamiltonian dynamics
has a higher error than floating point precision.

>>
>> Does anyone else on the list have experience with this?
>>
>> Did you test gradients for summation? Writing custom
>> gradients is critical for speed, but the gradients need to be
>> tested even if they're not custom. You should just be able
>> to use the gradient already there for sum.
> I've done, but I sadly lack knowledge to extract useful information from them.

You basically want to implement a complex summation
so that the gradients are done in the same way as for
sum(), but the value is calculated to higher precision.
In a sum(), the partial is just 1 for all of the components,
so there's really no more precision to be gained there.

>> Also, which signatures did you go with for sum()? It
>> should probably work over the same types as sort: real[],
>> int[], vector and row_vector.
> I tried a lot of different ways, but I decided to use just a single eigen vector to sum.
>
> vector [nZeros] summads;
> for (i in 1:nZeros)
> summands[i] <- log1p_exp(-zeta0[i]-exp(eta0[i]));
> 1 ~ bernoulli_logit(zeta0);
>
> yy1 ~ poisson_log(eta1);
> 0 ~ bernoulli_logit(zeta1);

What I meant is that if you implement kahan_sum(), you probably
want to implement it for real[], vector, and row-vector. Forget
what I said about int[], because you won't get any extra precision.

>> Could you perhaps break these into two separate pull requests
>> (sort/rank vs. summation).
> I started them in two different branches and it looks like it was a wise decision after all.

Great. Send us the pull request for sort() and rank() when
you have them. Just please make sure to run fairly extensive
tests. Testing these functions is usually harder than writing
them, so it's not doing us much of a favor to write the function without
extensive testing. For sort, you'd want to test zero size arrays/vectors
as input, and cases where all the numbers are the same, and some random
ones. There's no issue with gradients here because neither rank() nor
sort() have gradients to calculate.

- Bob
